items.body: Grammy-nominated guitarist Alex Wintz is not only a frequent performer, both with his own group and with artists such as the trumpeters Etienne Charles and Jeremy Pelt and trombonist Nick Finzer, but also an educator on the faculty of the New Jersey Performing Arts Center Jazz for Teens program and a clever composer. Collage features six excellent original tunes along with the jazz standard "The Shadow of Your Smile" and George Harrison's "Isn't It A Pity" and follows Wintz's two prior releases as a leader, LifeCycle (Culture Shock Music, 2017) and the very well-regarded Live To Tape (Outside in Music, 2020). Wintz's outstanding band on this date—all of whom, like the leader, trained at the Berklee College of Music and/or Julliard School—features bassist Matt Penman, nimble drummer Jimmy Macbride and pianist Victor Gould. Collage is a continually engaging album of superb compositions played with taste, groove and swing. Wintz gets a beautiful, pellucid tone from his Collings semi-hollow, heard immediately in album opener "Pondhop," inspired by the guitarist's international travels. Gould sits out this one, allowing Macbride's prominent tom accents and snare cross-sticking to drive this blues- based tune with a sunny West African twist to its prominent melody. The addition of Gould's piano vamp gives the gently swinging "Apt. 3C" a melancholy underpinning over which Wintz weaves a wistful melody that seems to invoke memories of past homes while moving into a new one. When Penman's deep-toned bass moves into a walking pattern under Gould's beautiful solo, Macbride's swing becomes jaunty, and the leader's own solo develops into one of his best on the record. Album highlight, "Innings Eater," begins with a meaty bass solo before settling into a wicked 5/4 groove eliciting wonderful interaction between the trio of Wintz, Penman, and Macbride. Special mention here should be made of the drummer's beautifully-tuned and well-recorded kit, with every subtle tom roll and hi-hat dynamic clear and present. Gould's piano returns for the bouncy "Better Half," dedicated to—who else?—Wintz's wife Francesca. It is a lovely tune of muted riffs, harmonically rich chord progressions and well-placed pauses that sound like the punctuation at the end of the conversation's sentences. In "The Wheels of Justice," a kind of modified blues waltz for the core trio, Wintz puts on a clinic of classic modern jazz guitar playing, pausing towards the end to give Penman and a chance to shine in his subtle solo before trading fours with Macbride. Complementing Wintz's excellent original tunes is a refreshingly funky take on Johnny Mandel's "The Shadow of Your Smile" and "Isn't It A Pity," in which the core trio avoids the rather dirge-like feel of Harrison's original, instead adopting a wry groove that will have listeners dancing the despair away. Deserving of a wide hearing, Collage is a superb jazz guitar record featuring Wintz's memorable tunes played with finesse by a talented, sympathetic band.

items.body: Picture this: Having assembled a supporting cast, finalized the playlist and booked a studio, you are ready to make the debut recording as leader of your own ensemble, only to learn that, hours earlier, said studio in East Lansing, Michigan, had been devastated by a tornado. That is exactly what happened to trombonist Eli Howell in May 2025. Fortunately, thanks to some quick thinking and deft maneuvering by album producer Michael Dease and others, a room was found at Howell's alma mater, Michigan State University, and the recording session went on as planned, without the usual isolation or overdubs, thus providing the sort of immediacy that was the norm in early-day studio sessions. It was not the first time that Howell had faced and overcome adversity. In 2023, he was diagnosed with focal dystonia, a neurological movement disorder that forced him to stop playing trombone for a year. Once past that, he saddled up again and was looking forward to recording with his sextet when the studio abruptly disappeared. Undaunted, Howell and his companions changed the location and started anew. The result of their efforts is a rather mixed bag whose several highlights serve to overshadow those moments that are less engaging. The session shines brightest on the standard "Alone Together," bassist Rodney Whitaker's well-grooved "For Garrison," Howell's high-stepping "One for Steve" (for fellow trombonist Steve Davis), the graceful "Dear Helen" (written for his great-grandmother), and Raul De Souza's rollicking finale, "A Vontade Mesmo." Howell's valve trombone duel with Dease on "A Vontade Mesmo" is especially impressive, as are Sharel Cassity's exquisite flute work on "One for Helen" and the snug group dynamics on "Alone Together" and "One for Steve," with incisive solos by Howell, Cassity, Whitaker, pianist Xavier Davis and trumpeter Brian Lynch, an added bonus. There were two recording sessions, three days apart, with alto saxophonist Thomas Noble, pianist Miki Hayama, bassist Langston Kitchen and drummer Colleen Clark replacing the core group on "A Clear Day" and "A Vontade Mesmo." Trombonist Wycliffe Gordon makes a guest appearance on his composition "I Remember Al" (a tribute to the late trombonist Al Grey), trying his best (and largely succeeding) with voice, mutes and other effects to make the trombone sound like anything but a trombone. Howell shares center stage with Lynch and alto Cassity on the album's nimble opening number, Jerry Bock and Sheldon Harnick's "Matchmaker," from the Broadway musical Fiddler on the Roof. As noted, an album whose high points readily outweigh any lesser moments, and one that is definitely worth your time and consideration.

items.body: In giving this album a listen, it is difficult not to jump between the original recordings of the great Blossom Dearie, and those newly recorded by modern-day pianist/vocalist Dawn Clement. After all, those who have followed Clement's career have heard the comparisons between the two, particularly the vocal style that those critiquing Dearie referred to as "distinctive," "light," and "girlish." The separator here is that Dearie, while lauded for her original piano style, is more renowned for her colorful, poetic vocals. Clement has thrived in both ways, but is perhaps better known for her powerful, rhythmic and harmonically brilliant original work on piano. The vocal side of her artistry features a wide-ranging, pitch- perfect instrument that has put the finishing touches on the "unique" part of her musical profile. All of this being said, it would seem likely then that Dear Ms. Dearie (Origin, 2026) would be a satisfying listen, and indeed, it is. There is no dressing things up here, as Clement works her way through fifteen tunes favored by Dearie, with an all-star presence in the studio to assist. Bassist John Clayton and drummer Jeff Hamilton are the perfect complement to this project, able to keep the session swinging at any tempo and in any time signature. Clement's Colorado mate Steve Kovalcheck jumps in on guitar to complete a live-in-the-studio sound that pulls you in for a more intimate listen. "The Gentleman is a Dope" leads things off, with Clement taking the tune in on piano, establishing the easy swing of her bandmates. Clement does not skip a beat, entering the fray singing the first verse. She gathers things together following Kovalcheck's breakneck solo, before releasing the flow of the melody to the end of the tune. If there is a parallel for starters between the artist and subject here, it is the feeling that the piano and the voice are one thing, of one mind. There is a clear advantage of a singer accompanying themselves, knowing best how to complement the vocal component of their artistry. There is no overplaying or other missteps to be concerned with. Clement's voice darts between notes of the melody in the same bop cadence of her melodic playing on piano. The lead tune reveals the sincerity that takes a perfectly solid performance and makes it exceptional. "Figure 8" is a tune familiar to those who grew up in the early 1970s watching Saturday morning cartoons. As the theme song for the educational "Schoolhouse Rock" series, youngsters were exposed to Dearie singing Bob McDonough's wispy math- inspired lyrics. Accompanied by the full chords of Kovalcheck and bassist Clayton's elegant bow work, Clement lightly escorts the tune to a higher tempo, adding scant comping while Kovalcheck carries the harmonic load. "Once Upon a Summertime" is the title tune from Dearie's 1959 Verve Records classic. It is here that Clement's work is illuminated visually, the nostalgic lyrics brightly revealed like landscapes captured by an artist on a bright sunny day. Clement works in tandem with Clayton, offering a stunning solo that flows out of her dynamic sense of emotion within harmony. The ballad may just be the high point of the session, although it is presented as the twelfth track of the fifteen. No tip of the cap to Dearie would be complete without a version of the David Frishberg penned "I'm Hip," again with lyrics from McDonough. Clayton's walking bass line and Hamilton's sublime brushwork lay down the foundation for Clement's swinging, fleeting treatment of every syllable. Kovalcheck's work throughout the session is perfectly complementary to the other chordal instrument, allowing both he and Clement to play unforced, with an emphasis on beauty and intimacy. On all fifteen tunes, Clement does not have to force a darn thing, her natural musical self fits so perfectly into the spirit of Dearie's work and legacy. While adhering to the simple, straight-ahead setting present on the original classic recordings, Clement makes the music quite naturally hers, perhaps finally eschewing the label of being a pianist who also sings. Those in the know are aware that this has never been the case. Dearie once stated that she did not like singing or playing piano separately. It feels that way throughout the playlist that Clement offers here. Dear Ms. Dearie may not be Clement's best album to date in terms of her career as a highly original jazz pianist. It is indeed a departure from her preceding trio effort, Delight (Origin, 2025), with Buster Williams and Matt Wilson—but it may be the best manifestation of her complete musical presence revealed.

items.body: The connection(s) between pianist-composers Satoko Fujii and Myra Melford transcend the usual truisms. Not kindred spirits in creativity or even mirror images in technique, the pair are more like twin sisters of different artistic mothers, distinctly their own individuals in style yet complementary as such in almost ineffable ways. Hence this album title, a Japanese term referring to a heart-to-heart conversation between intimate friends, fittingly suggests a deep, meaningful dialogue. Katarahi is the duo's second collaboration, but as noted by discerning essayist Ed Hazell, it has been two decades since the performance captured on Under The Water (Libra, 2009). Unlike the wholly improvised predecessor, the second enterprise consists of the two playing each other's original compositions, having mutually agreed designated material furthers the instrumental vocabulary they can bring into play. "Interlude I" thus acts as a gateway into this slightly more than 51 minutes from a September 2024 performance at Jazzfestival Liebnitz, Austria. As recorded by Norbert Stadlhofer, then mixed and mastered by Maikol Seminatore, the music ebbs and flows from ghostly rounds of notes to ringing lines, then back again, during which developments none touch in overlay (much less collide). Approaching each extremely cautiously, Fujii and Melford consciously or unconsciously reveal the magnificent potential of the piano as a musical instrument; in so doing, they stipulate its attraction to such great minds as theirs to devote a life's work to its exploration. Perhaps that is why a piece of Fujii's titled "Signpost" shows up early in the song sequence. Or, more appropriately, why temperance and patience earmarks both musicians' approach throughout: on "Pairs," rumbles from deep within echo around strings plucked and tweaked amidst emphatic strikes to the keys. And the track immediately following, "Chalk," reiterates the reality these two are utilizing a percussion device, as the roiling swirls of impacted notes span the dynamic register. The slow motion conclusion of that piece suggests the instinctual pacing Fujii and Melford apply during Katarahi. The selection to follow, "Kaiwa," is the longest of the seven at 10 minutes, 35 seconds, its placement ratifying that the pair are all warmed up and ready for some rollicking fun. Indeed, there is a palpable joy emanating from this dual action proceeding up and down the ivories before more contemplative interludes commence. Here is where the dialogue redefines the vaunted trope about telepathy between like-minded musicians deep in the midst of performance, particularly when it is occurring on the stage. The rise and fall in intensity there turns into a microcosm of this entire program as it enters the homestretch via "IV"; repetition such as this has its purpose, arising only from elliptical afterthoughts to exchanges seconds prior. In this nuanced approach, Fujii and Melford are, in effect, tying together the loose ends from the otherwise densely embroidered threads they have sewn together to this point. It is a supreme statement of the logic inherent in this collaboration, thus rendering "From Sometime" an objective observation on the chemistry these musicians have just demonstrated so fully. The exultation Fujii and Melford display in the rousing finish compels the audience to respond in kind and rightly so.

items.body: There is a moment on "Tea Horse Road," the album's fourth track, where the saxophone drops to a near whisper and the percussion seems to breathe rather than strike. You realize you are not listening to two musicians from opposite sides of the world so much as two people who have agreed, without a word, on exactly how much silence costs. Lao Dan grew up in Northeastern China near the North Korean border. He showed enough early talent on saxophone and bamboo flute to earn a place at conservatory, then walked away from it. He studied dizi formally in Beijing and later at Shenyang Conservatory before turning toward avant-garde jazz and free improvisation around 2013. What he took from that training was not obedience. It was control: a deep physical understanding of breath through a tube, and an instinct for space that most Western free players spend decades trying to locate. Barcelona-based Vasco Trilla came to the drums late, at nineteen, through progressive rock and metal. He worked his way outward through jazz, African music, and free improvisation. He has since appeared on more than a hundred recordings for labels including NoBusiness, Clean Feed, and Cuneiform. He plays like a man who understands that the wrong note at the right moment is still the wrong note. The seven tracks here, from the opener "You Are You" through the closing "Nobodies Are Going to Sleep," feel less like a set list than a field journal. Lao Dan moves between tenor saxophone and dizi (Chinese flute), changing not just tone but altitude. Trilla generates rhythm without always generating a pulse, which is a different and harder skill. On "Fire Boy," Dan's flute cuts upward in tight spirals while Trilla accelerates with the controlled intensity of someone who knows exactly how hot to let things get. "Tea Horse Road," named for the ancient trade route connecting Yunnan to Tibet, sits at the emotional center. It is patient, unresolved, and genuinely rooted. The drummer shakes what sounds like a string of small cymbals while giving Dan a wide, open background. As the piece heats up, the intensity feels both grounded and spiritually convincing. The closing track thins out slowly until you are not sure whether you are still listening or simply sitting in the room where the music happened. It is a good place to leave things.

items.body: In this recording by bassist, composer and bandleader Ben Wolfe, titled Any Time After Now, there is a quiet assurance, with nothing straining for effect or feeling manufactured. Recorded in a single studio day alongside vibraphonist Joel Ross, pianist Sullivan Fortner, tenor saxophonist Chris Lewis and drummer Aaron Kimmel, the album spans ten tracks of original Wolfe compositions and exhibits a natural cohesion that reflects musicians deeply attuned to one another. The opener, "Any Time After Now," swings with effortless authority. Wolfe's bass lines move with confidence beneath Lewis and Ross's contributions, while Fortner brings a strong rhythmic sense to the tune. Kimmel takes an imaginative turn on his kit, adding to the bebop narrative. "Waltz II" is striking for its delicacy. Buoyed by Wolfe's deep tone and steady beat, Ross and Fortner interact with arresting sensitivity, each phrase answered by the other. "Blues" evokes a hazy, after-hours atmosphere. Lewis delivers an expressive performance, smoky, relaxed, and soulful. Ross follows with an improvisation rich in harmonic nuance, and Fortner settles into a blues statement grounded in groove and touch. "5/4 Groove" unfolds as Kimmel shapes the asymmetrical pulse with ease, while Fortner crafts an extended meditation brimming with momentum and tension. Wolfe's solo is a highlight, lyrical, poised, and deeply musical. Wolfe, an unusual musician who associates music with color, shape and texture, writes compositions that carry visual weight. The music shifts between shadows, light, density and openness with remarkable fluidity. The result is a performance in which the band knows exactly how to inhabit these spaces. "Down with Gravity" brings sharp angles and earthy funk. Wolfe and Kimmel work hand in glove, while Lewis stretches out with a harmonic vocabulary that yields clarity of ideas. There is a real bite here without sacrificing sophistication. "Always Four" opens with an assertive flourish from Kimmel, then settles into tightly focused exchanges between Ross and Fortner. Kimmel is back on board with crisp playing, taking the tune out as each idea feels purposeful. "Til The Next Time" is a silky bossa nova that glides effortlessly into the ear. Ross, in full vibrato, phrases beautifully over Wolfe's subtle plucking. Fortner and Kimmel keep everything light and pleasant. The closing bonus track, "Green," swings with optimism and zest. Ross and Fortner carry the instrumental load with a keen sense of musical drama, while Wolfe and Kimmel deliver sharply etched pulses. The number offers a clear picture of Wolfe's melodic, thoughtful, and generous compositional voice.

items.body: Storybook: The Music Of Mark Miller is at one level the unfolding narrative of its 10 musical selections. At another, it is a tale about its primary author, Mark Miller, who traced his journey from {jny: Racine}} to New York City with his previous release Mark Miller: The Return Of Slide Huxtable (Slide Huxtable, 2008)—a long road that is a serious jazz player's dream of making it in the Big Apple. But most of all, it is a compelling reminder to listeners everywhere that the Manhattan jazz experience is incomplete without a trip to hear the Birdland Big Band. Birdland's original, long defunct basement club at "The Jazz Corner of the World" (Broadway and 52nd) now occupies a bigger mid-town area, bounded on the north by Jazz at Lincoln Center (60 St.) and, on the south, by the "new" Birdland (44th St). Start at 52nd St., walk 8 blocks in either direction, and you are there. But which direction? Is there a significant difference? Some observers have suggested that big band music from the north references the genius of Duke Ellington, whereas the sounds to the south are aligned with the swing of Count Basie. Yet "Storybook," the eponymous title of the album's Grammy-nominated first track, sounds like something else entirely. Miller—much of whose "schooling" was on the road as trombonist-composer with the Minneapolis-based jazz group, The Motion Poets—has constructed a brilliant sonic gateway that owes as much to Bach and Bartok as to Ellington or Count Basie. Starting with a stately 3-note descending motif, the composition builds on that figure with rich harmonies and vibrant dynamics, answered by an ascending counter-melody played by the lower brass. Soon, the entire sequence is repeated, with the addition of creative commentary from Brandon Lee's flugelhorn. After a sharply articulated, vigorously syncopated version of the primary motif, Kenny Barron's infectious "Water Lily." Unlike earlier recorded versions that are slower and light-spirited, the tune here is taken at a driving tempo with accompaniment by piano and drums that borders on the intrusive (likely due to an over-hot audio mix-down). Besides an inventive piano solo by Kenny Ascher, the piece showcases the commanding artistry of saxophonist Troy Roberts, whose closing cadenza balances impressive pyrotechnics with satisfying musical taste. Next, the standard, "Tenderly," lightens the mood with a sprightly version of a waltz that, with the notable exception of Bill Evans' up-tempo version, usually receives the slow, pensive reading of Rosemary Clooney or the even slower 4/4 versions by Sara Vaughn and Billie Holiday. Miller's arrangement exhibits remarkable attention to detail, replete with spiraling flutes that simulate butterflies to complement the spring setting for vocalist Nicole Zuraitis. Brief solos by Sam Dillon (a. sax) and Raul Agraz (trpt) fit seamlessly with the colorful seasonal mix. Miller's own "Chorale and Alleluia" is as contemplative and celebratory as its title might suggest. It features the percussive thunder of Chris Smith, who will also be critical to the driving samba rhythm of Chick Corea's "Spain." Tom Harrell's "Sail Away" is an inviting melody launched without affectation by Glenn Drewes' reassuring flugel. After band director David DeJesus' soprano sax has taken control of the cruise, Drews resumes his storytelling by, in effect, shutting off the engine (i.e., piano, bass, drums) and allowing only the sounds of wind and water for several choruses—the pulse of the band sans rhythm section. It is tempting to continue with a play-by-play analysis if only to identify the soloists in an ensemble with no weak links. The Birdland Band is "deep" with talent, each player capable of assuming solo duties on any given night. Take, for example, "WTF," in which trombonist/composer Miller resumes the cruise with a witty trombone exchange between James Burton III and Sara Jacovino, one that recalls the musical conversations by J.J. Johnson and Jay and Kai Winding. The last third of the program is cued up by the standard "Close Your Eyes," which opens with Zuraitis close to the mic as she fashions a soft, pitch-perfect, improvised chorus before yielding to an Ascher piano solo that swings with the sure-fingered authority of Wynton Kelly. Following a good-humored, equally swinging turn by bass trombonist, James Borowski, Zuraitis re-enters for an "out" chorus that soon becomes "far-out," her voice rising in pitch and volume to the level of a Maynard Ferguson set-closer. It works because the vocalist implants herself in the trumpet section, rising to a powerful climax as the job requires. Finally, we receive a healthy reminder that "swing" does not require a thing except a ride cymbal and a hi-hat. (If only audio engineers could figure out a way to include the shimmer of a Zildjian in their mastering of live sounds.) Rodrigo de Arunez's "Concierto" and Corea's "Spain" are worthy additions to those already in print. And they are among the most "honest," avoiding orchestral instruments (French horns, double reeds, tympani, etc.) as well as electronic devices (Fender Rhodes, phaser boxes, onboard modulating effects). The result is a focus that remains fixed on the music, not the gear. And then there is the memorable close-out for "Spain"—an ascending Miller bass-line that, in effect, resolves a sparking, fractious debate between big band and drums, then between sections within the ensemble. "The DoubleDown," the last track of the regular program, evokes a Sunday night gospel meeting with its inviting singalong melody in ¾. The primary preacher is Ron Wilkins, whose testifying on plunger-muted trombone produces a meditative bass solo by Noriko Ueda. But rather than exit quietly, the congregation is led back by saxophones to the main theme, then a sudden stop and lift to a new key for a final testament by Mark Miller's emphatic postlude on trombone. Church is out, but the congregation's spirits crave more action. "Nonsense," an original shuffle-rhythm blues composed by Miller and Zuraitis, answers the need to sustain the sense of play embedded in every true storybook. Zuraitis delivers a nonsensical lyric in the strongest musical terms, conversing over stop-time chords with Miller's and Wilkins' vocal trombones. Next, she handles "vocalese" lines in tight unison with tricky instrumental figures. Finally, there is a vocal exchange, over pedal-tone bass, between the entire band and its girl singer, who has the last word: "Nonsense? Come on, whatever gets you. Small wonder that, after hearing a call like that, visitors are setting aside Friday nights for a return to Birdland.

items.body: At a time when economics often dictates the size and scope of a jazz group, adding a guitarist to a typical piano-bass-drums trio makes a world of difference. And when said guitarist is Peter Bernstein, the difference is even more pronounced. That gives bassist Harvie S a clear headstart on Bright Dawn, a modest studio date with Bernstein broadening the usual trio setting on the bassist's 21st recording as leader of his own ensemble—the first, however, following a 15-year hiatus. The other members of Harvie's group, each of whom plays a pivotal role, are pianist Miki Hayama (Fender Rhodes on "Ghosts of Havana" and "Voice in the Sky") and drummer Matt Wilson who introduces and sparks the perky "I've Got Rhythm and Blues." That is one of Harvie's eight compositions, escorting Bob Dorough's playful "Devil May Care" and Chick Corea's sunny "Humpty Dumpty." And therein lies the session's most problematic aspect. Even though decent and well-intentioned, Harvie's compositions are, to be frank, several lengthy strides away from memorable. While that may be traced in part to the group's makeup and Harvie S's resolve to lead the way, the fact remains that the success of any collective enterprise, regardless of size or shape, rests in large measure on its choice of material, and most of the songs on Bright Dawn simply don't measure up, even with Bernstein on board to help enliven them. Harvie must be given props for naming one of his themes "Navalny" (and enhancing it with arco and string bass) but even that melody seems tame when compared to what comes next, the spunky "Rhythm and Blues," one of the session's few high spots. Hayama is an impressive soloist, as is Bernstein, and their expertise must be noted. That is not, however, nearly enough to raise Bright Dawn above the norm.
